Incorporating SLOOS evidence shifts the tone modestly more cautious than a pure “hawkish hold”:

- Broad-based tightening: Banks reported tighter standards and terms across C&I (all firm sizes, syndicated and non-syndicated), CRE (construction, land development, multifamily, nonfarm nonresidential), RRE (GSE-eligible, government, QM/non-QM jumbo and non-jumbo), and consumer credit (credit cards, auto, HELOCs). Subprime segments showed notably weaker demand.
- Weaker loan demand: Demand softened across C&I and household credit categories, reinforcing a credit-driven drag on activity.
- Drivers and risks: Reduced risk tolerance, higher funding costs/liquidity concerns, and collateral/covenant tightening align with financial-stability sensitivities (notably CRE exposures at regional banks).

Implication for the statement: The SLOOS corroborates the Committee’s line that “tighter credit conditions… are likely to weigh on economic activity, hiring, and inflation,” suggesting a stronger prospective credit headwind than the statement alone conveys. With QT continuing to firm broader financial conditions, the policy stance remains inflation-wary and data-dependent but is tempered by tightening credit supply and softer demand. Netting these, the stance leans closer to neutral than hawkish.
